etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old French converser, from Latin conversor (“live, have dealings with”).

definitions.definition: (formal, intransitive) To talk; to engage in conversation.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iv]:
quote.text: Companions […]  That do converse and waste the time together.

quote.citation: 1695, C[harles] A[lphonse] du Fresnoy, translated by John Dryden, De Arte Graphica. The Art of Painting, […], London:  […]  J[ohn] Heptinstall for W. Rogers, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: We had conversed so often on that subject.

definitions.definition: (followed by with) To keep company; to hold intimate intercourse; to commune.

quote.citation: a. 1749 (date written), James Thomson, “Summer”, in The Seasons, London:  […]  A[ndrew] Millar, and sold by Thomas Cadell, […], published 1768, →OCLC:
quote.text: To seek the distant hills, and there converse With nature.
But to converse with heaven — This is not easy.

quote.citation: 1819 December 20 (indicated as 1820), Walter Scott, Ivanhoe; a Romance. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), Edinburgh:  […]  Archibald Constable and Co.; London: Hurst, Robinson, and Co. […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Conversing with the world, we use the world's fashions.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To have knowledge of something, from long talk or study.

quote.citation: 1689 (indicated as 1690), [John Locke], An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding. […], London:  […]  Eliz[abeth] Holt, for Thomas Basset, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: according as the objects they converse with afford greater or less variety

definitions.definition: (now literary) Free verbal interchange of thoughts or views; conversation; chat.

quote.citation: 1727, [Edward Young], “Satire V. On Women.”, in Love of Fame, the Universal Passion. In Seven Characteristical Satires, 4th edition, London:  […]  J[acob] and R[ichard] Tonson […], published 1741, →OCLC:
quote.text: Twice ere the sun descends, with zeal inspir'd, / From the vain converse of the world retir'd, / She reads the psalms and chapters for the day  […]

quote.citation: 1764 December 24 (indicated as 1765), Onuphrio Muralto, translated by William Marshal [pseudonyms; Horace Walpole], chapter III, in The Castle of Otranto, […], London:  […]  Tho[mas] Lownds […], →OCLC, page 93:
quote.text: [R]eturn to thy maſter, and tell him, e'er vve liquidate our differences by the ſvvord, Manfred vvould hold ſome converſe vvith him.

quote.citation: 1834, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], chapter XVI, in Francesca Carrara. […], volume I, London: Richard Bentley, […], (successor to Henry Colburn), →OCLC, page 177:
quote.text: She had around her gay converse, in which she had no share; and laughter, in which she was little tempted to join.

quote.citation: 1919, Saki [pseudonym; Hector Hugh Munro], “The Disappearance of Crispina Umerleigh”, in R[othay] R[eynolds], editor, The Toys of Peace and Other Papers. […], London: John Lane, The Bodley Head […], →OCLC:
quote.text: In a first-class carriage of a train speeding Balkanward across the flat, green Hungarian plain, two Britons sat in friendly, fitful converse.

quote.citation: 1930, Norman Lindsay, Redheap, Sydney, N.S.W.: Ure Smith, published 1965, →OCLC, page 26:
quote.text: [S]uch was the aberration of mind attending converse with a successful draper.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin conversus (“turned around”), past participle of converto (“turn about”).

definitions.definition: Opposite; reversed in order or relation; reciprocal.
(logic) Of a proposition or theorem consisting of a statement of the form "If A is true, then B is true", the statement "If B is true, then A is true" which need not be equivalent to the first one.
(semantics) One of a pair of terms that name or describe a relationship from opposite perspectives; converse antonym; relational antonym.
